name: RC Discharge Voltage
description: Computes the voltage V0×e^(-t/(R×C)) across a capacitor discharging through a resistor after time t. The voltage decays exponentially with time constant R×C from its initial value V0.
notes: Time t, resistance R, and capacitance C must use consistent SI units so that R×C is in seconds. After one time constant the voltage falls to about 37 percent of V0.

name: RC Charging Voltage
description: Computes the voltage V0×(1-e^(-t/(R×C))) across a capacitor charging toward supply voltage V0 through a resistor after time t. It rises exponentially with time constant R×C.
notes: Use consistent SI units so that R×C is in seconds. After one time constant the capacitor reaches about 63 percent of the supply voltage V0.

name: RL Rising Current
description: Computes the current I0×(1-e^(-t×R/L)) rising toward its final value I0 in an RL circuit after time t. The current builds up exponentially with time constant L/R.
notes: Resistance R, inductance L, and time t must use consistent SI units. After one time constant L/R the current reaches about 63 percent of its final value I0.

name: RL Decaying Current
description: Computes the current I0×e^(-t×R/L) decaying from its initial value I0 in an RL circuit after time t. The current falls exponentially with time constant L/R.
notes: Resistance R, inductance L, and time t must use consistent SI units. After one time constant L/R the current falls to about 37 percent of its initial value I0.

name: RC Low-Pass Cutoff Frequency
description: Computes the -3 dB cutoff frequency 1/(2×pi×R×C) of an RC low-pass filter with resistance R and capacitance C. Above this frequency the filter increasingly attenuates the signal.
notes: Resistance R is in ohms and capacitance C in farads, giving frequency in hertz. At the cutoff the output amplitude is 1/sqrt(2) of the input.

name: RL Cutoff Frequency
description: Computes the -3 dB cutoff frequency R/(2×pi×L) of an RL filter with resistance R and inductance L. It marks the frequency at which the reactance equals the resistance.
notes: Resistance R is in ohms and inductance L in henries, giving frequency in hertz. The corresponding time constant of the circuit is L/R.

name: Parallel RLC Quality Factor
description: Computes the quality factor R×sqrt(C/L) of a parallel RLC resonant circuit with resistance R, capacitance C, and inductance L. A higher Q means a sharper, more selective resonance.
notes: All values are in SI units and the result is dimensionless. Note this parallel-circuit form differs from the series RLC quality factor, which is (1/R)×sqrt(L/C).

name: Inductor Quality Factor
description: Computes the quality factor 2×pi×f×L/R of an inductor at frequency f, comparing its reactance to its series resistance R. A higher Q indicates lower relative losses.
notes: Frequency f is in hertz, L in henries, and R in ohms, giving a dimensionless result. Q generally rises with frequency but R itself grows at high frequency due to skin effect.

name: Capacitor Quality Factor
description: Computes the quality factor 1/(2×pi×f×R×C) of a capacitor at frequency f, comparing its reactance to its equivalent series resistance R. A higher Q means lower dielectric and resistive losses.
notes: Frequency f is in hertz, R (the ESR) in ohms, and C in farads, giving a dimensionless result. Q is the reciprocal of the loss tangent and decreases as frequency rises.

name: Neper Frequency of Series RLC
description: Computes the neper frequency (damping coefficient) of a series RLC circuit as R divided by twice the inductance L. This value, in 1/s, sets how fast the natural transient response decays.
notes: Applies to the series RLC topology; the parallel case uses 1/(2RC) instead. Compare with the resonant frequency to judge whether the circuit is under-, critically, or over-damped.

name: Characteristic Impedance of an LC Network
description: Gives the characteristic impedance of an LC network as the square root of inductance L divided by capacitance C. It represents the impedance that matches the network for maximum power transfer.
notes: L and C must be in henries and farads; the result is in ohms. This is a purely reactive-element ratio and ignores any series resistance or losses in real components.

name: RC Circuit Phase Angle
description: Calculates the phase angle between voltage and current in a series RC circuit as arctan(1/(2·pi·f·R·C)). The result, in radians, shows how far the current leads the applied voltage.
notes: Output is in radians; multiply by 180/pi for degrees. Valid for a simple series RC pair; the angle approaches pi/2 at low frequency and zero at high frequency.

name: RL Circuit Phase Angle
description: Calculates the phase angle of a series RL circuit as arctan(2·pi·f·L/R). The result, in radians, is the angle by which the voltage leads the current due to the inductive reactance.
notes: Output is in radians; convert to degrees with 180/pi. The angle rises toward pi/2 as frequency or inductance grows, since inductive reactance then dominates the resistance.

name: Transformer Impedance Ratio
description: Gives the impedance seen at the transformer primary as the secondary impedance Zs times the square of the primary-to-secondary turns ratio (Np/Ns)². It shows how a transformer scales impedance.
notes: Impedance transforms with the square of the turns ratio, not linearly. Assumes an ideal transformer with tight coupling and negligible winding losses or leakage.

name: 555 Astable Frequency
description: Estimates the output frequency of a 555 timer in astable mode as 1.44/((R1+2·R2)·C). This is the number of oscillation cycles per second set by the two resistors and the timing capacitor.
notes: The constant 1.44 equals 1/ln(2)/... approximated; valid for the standard astable wiring. Frequency is in hertz with R in ohms and C in farads; real 555 chips drift with supply and temperature.

name: 555 Astable Period
description: Gives the total oscillation period of a 555 astable circuit as 0.693·(R1+2·R2)·C, the time in seconds for one complete high-plus-low cycle of the output.
notes: 0.693 is ln(2); the period is the reciprocal of the astable frequency. R must be in ohms and C in farads; component tolerances shift the actual timing noticeably.

name: 555 Astable Duty Cycle
description: Computes the duty cycle of a standard 555 astable oscillator as (R1+R2)/(R1+2·R2), the fraction of each period the output stays high.
notes: Result is a fraction between 0.5 and 1; multiply by 100 for percent. The basic circuit cannot reach 50% because R1 is in the charge path but not the discharge path.

name: 555 Monostable Pulse Width
description: Gives the output pulse width of a 555 timer in monostable (one-shot) mode as 1.1·R·C, the duration in seconds the output stays high after a trigger.
notes: 1.1 equals ln(3); the width is independent of supply voltage. R must be in ohms and C in farads; large electrolytic capacitor leakage can shorten the actual pulse.

name: Quarter-Wave Antenna Length
description: Estimates the physical length of a quarter-wavelength antenna element as the speed of light (3e8 m/s) divided by four times the frequency f. The result is one quarter of the free-space wavelength in meters.
notes: Uses the free-space wavelength; real antennas need a velocity/shortening factor of about 0.95, making them slightly shorter. Frequency is in hertz.

name: Half-Wave Dipole Physical Length
description: Estimates the physical length of a half-wave dipole as 0.95·(3e8)/(2·f), the free-space half-wavelength multiplied by a 0.95 velocity factor to account for end effects.
notes: The 0.95 factor approximates real-conductor shortening; thicker elements need a smaller factor. Frequency is in hertz and the length is in meters, split between the two dipole arms.

name: Decibel Power Gain
description: Converts a power ratio into decibels as 10·log10(P2/P1), where P2 is the output power and P1 the input power. Positive results mean gain and negative results mean loss.
notes: This is the power form using a factor of 10; voltage or current ratios use 20 instead. Both powers must share the same unit, and P1 must be nonzero and positive.

name: Non-Inverting Amplifier Gain
description: Gives the closed-loop voltage gain of a non-inverting op-amp configuration as 1 + Rf/Rin, where Rf is the feedback resistor and Rin the resistor to ground. The output stays in phase with the input.
notes: Gain is dimensionless and always at least 1. Assumes an ideal op-amp; real gain is limited by the finite gain-bandwidth product at higher frequencies.

name: Inverting Amplifier Gain
description: Gives the closed-loop gain of an inverting op-amp configuration as -Rf/Rin. The negative sign shows the output is inverted (180° out of phase) relative to the input.
notes: The result is negative by design, denoting phase inversion; its magnitude is the gain. Assumes an ideal op-amp with the non-inverting input grounded and a virtual ground at the summing node.

name: Closed-Loop Gain with Negative Feedback
description: Computes the closed-loop gain of a negative-feedback amplifier as A0/(1 + A0·beta), where A0 is the open-loop gain and beta the feedback fraction. Feedback trades raw gain for stability and linearity.
notes: When A0·beta is much greater than 1, the gain approaches 1/beta and becomes nearly independent of A0. Both A0 and beta are dimensionless.

name: Slew-Rate Limited Bandwidth
description: Gives the full-power bandwidth of an op-amp as SR/(2·pi·Vp), where SR is the slew rate and Vp the peak output voltage. Above this frequency a full-amplitude sine wave becomes slew-rate distorted.
notes: This large-signal bandwidth is distinct from the small-signal bandwidth. Slew rate is in volts per second and peak voltage is the amplitude, not the peak-to-peak value.

name: Gain-Bandwidth Product
description: Computes the gain-bandwidth product of an amplifier as the closed-loop gain A times its bandwidth BW. For a single-pole amplifier this product is approximately constant, so higher gain means proportionally less bandwidth.
notes: Valid for dominant single-pole (first-order) amplifiers; the product equals the unity-gain frequency. Gain is dimensionless and bandwidth is in hertz.

name: Wheatstone Bridge Unknown Resistance
description: Finds the unknown resistance in a balanced Wheatstone bridge as R2·R3/R1, using the three known arm resistors. At balance no current flows through the galvanometer.
notes: Valid only at bridge balance (zero detector current); the ratio must match the bridge arrangement. All resistances share the same unit, so the result comes out in ohms.

name: Wien Bridge Oscillator Frequency
description: Gives the oscillation frequency of a Wien bridge oscillator as 1/(2·pi·R·C), assuming equal resistors and equal capacitors in the frequency-selective network.
notes: Assumes the two RC pairs are matched; unequal components shift the formula. Frequency is in hertz with R in ohms and C in farads, and the amplifier needs a gain of exactly 3 to sustain oscillation.

name: Colpitts Oscillator Frequency
description: Computes the resonant frequency of a Colpitts oscillator as 1/(2·pi·sqrt(L·Cseries)), where the two capacitors combine in series as C1·C2/(C1+C2). This sets the LC tank oscillation frequency.
notes: The capacitive divider forms the feedback; use the series combination, not the sum. Frequency is in hertz with L in henries and capacitances in farads.

name: Hartley Oscillator Frequency
description: Computes the resonant frequency of a Hartley oscillator as 1/(2·pi·sqrt((L1+L2)·C)), where the two inductors add in series to tune the tank circuit with the capacitor C.
notes: Assumes no mutual coupling between the coils; magnetic coupling would add a 2M term to the total inductance. Frequency is in hertz with inductances in henries and C in farads.

name: Johnson-Nyquist Noise Voltage
description: Computes the RMS thermal (Johnson-Nyquist) noise voltage of a resistor as sqrt(4·kB·T·R·B), arising from the random thermal motion of charge carriers over a measurement bandwidth B.
notes: Uses the Boltzmann constant 1.38e-23 J/K; temperature must be absolute (kelvin). The result is an RMS value and depends on bandwidth, not on the signal or current.

name: Shot Noise Current
description: Computes the RMS shot noise current as sqrt(2·q·I·B), where q is the elementary charge (1.6e-19 C), I the DC current, and B the bandwidth. It stems from the discrete nature of charge crossing a junction.
notes: Applies to currents crossing a potential barrier such as a diode or transistor junction, not to simple ohmic conductors. The result is an RMS value over bandwidth B.

name: Rectifier Ripple Voltage
description: Estimates the peak-to-peak ripple voltage on a rectifier filter capacitor as Iload/(f·C), where Iload is the load current, f the ripple frequency, and C the filter capacitance.
notes: This is a linear-discharge approximation valid for small ripple; f is the ripple frequency (twice the line frequency for a full-wave rectifier), not the line frequency itself.

name: Thermal Voltage
description: Computes the thermal voltage of a semiconductor junction as kB·T/q, using the Boltzmann constant and elementary charge. It equals about 25.85 mV at 300 K and scales linearly with absolute temperature.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin; the result is in volts. This quantity appears in the diode and transistor exponential current equations and is often abbreviated VT.

name: Shockley Diode Current
description: Computes diode current from the Shockley equation as Is·(exp(V/(nf·Vt)) - 1), where Is is the saturation current, V the forward voltage, nf the ideality factor, and Vt the thermal voltage.
notes: The exponential grows steeply, so small voltage changes cause large current swings. Ignores series resistance and high-injection effects, which flatten the curve at large forward voltage.

name: Parallel LC Tank Dynamic Impedance
description: Gives the dynamic (resonant) impedance of a parallel LC tank as L/(R·C), where R is the series coil resistance. This is the high, purely resistive impedance the tank presents at resonance.
notes: Valid at the resonant frequency for a coil with small series resistance R. All quantities in SI units give the result in ohms; larger coil resistance lowers the peak impedance.

name: Reflection Coefficient
description: Computes the voltage reflection coefficient at a transmission-line load as (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0), where ZL is the load impedance and Z0 the line characteristic impedance. It quantifies how much of a wave is reflected.
notes: For real impedances the result ranges from -1 to +1; a matched load (ZL = Z0) gives zero reflection. Complex impedances yield a complex coefficient not captured by this real-valued form.

name: Voltage Standing Wave Ratio
description: Converts the reflection coefficient magnitude G into the voltage standing wave ratio as (1 + G)/(1 - G). VSWR describes the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage along a mismatched transmission line.
notes: G is the magnitude of the reflection coefficient, between 0 and 1; VSWR ranges from 1 (perfect match) upward. As G approaches 1 the VSWR diverges toward infinity.

name: Coaxial Line Characteristic Impedance
description: Computes the characteristic impedance of a coaxial cable as (60/sqrt(er))·ln(b/a), where er is the dielectric relative permittivity, a the inner-conductor radius, and b the inner radius of the outer shield.
notes: a and b must share the same length unit since only their ratio matters; er is dimensionless. Assumes a lossless line with a homogeneous dielectric between the conductors.

name: Transmission Line Delay per Length
description: Gives the propagation delay per unit length of a transmission line as sqrt(L·C), using the inductance and capacitance per unit length. The result, in seconds per meter, is the reciprocal of the signal velocity.
notes: L and C here are per-length values (H/m and F/m), not lumped totals. Assumes a lossless line; multiply by the physical length to get the total propagation delay.

name: Delta-to-Wye Resistor Conversion
description: Converts a delta (triangle) resistor network to an equivalent wye (star) one, giving a wye branch resistance as Ra·Rb/(Ra+Rb+Rc) from the product of two adjacent delta resistors over the sum of all three.
notes: This gives one wye resistor; the other two follow by cycling which delta pair appears in the numerator. All three delta resistances must be in the same unit.

name: Maximum Power Transfer
description: Gives the maximum power deliverable to a load as Vs²/(4·R), where Vs is the source voltage and R the source resistance. This peak occurs when the load resistance equals the source resistance.
notes: Valid only at the matched condition (load = source resistance); at match, efficiency is just 50% because equal power dissipates in the source. Vs is in volts and R in ohms.

name: Damping Ratio of a Series RLC Circuit
description: Computes the damping ratio (zeta) of a series RLC circuit as (R/2)·sqrt(C/L). This dimensionless value governs the transient behavior: below 1 is underdamped, 1 is critical, above 1 is overdamped.
notes: Applies to the series RLC arrangement; the parallel case uses a reciprocal-form expression. The damping ratio is the reciprocal of twice the quality factor Q.
